div.p: Deep learning-based radiomics and machine learning for IDH-wild-type glioblastoma after maximal safe surgical resection: a call for prognostic assessment Lingmin Li, MD a , Zhenqiang Hao, MM b , Bo Li, MD b, * Dear Editor, Glioblastoma, a common primary malignant brain tumor [1] , which is characterized by a high recurrence rate, tumor cell penetration into the brain and rapid growth, with an average yearly age-adjusted incidence of is 3.19 per 100 000 persons. Treatment becomes more difficult when epigenetic and genetic changes interfere with important pathways regulating proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis. Patients with glioblastoma suffer a daunting prognosis, with a median overall survival (OS) of 15.6 months, even with extensive treatment plans that include chemoradiation and surgery. More than 90% of glioblastoma cases are of the isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wild-type kind, which has a very poor prognosis. Based on relevant risk variables, an accurate OS prediction is essential for early intervention.

Compared to routine pathological evaluation, imaging technique has the benefit of being able to identify the invasive, nonresectable components of glioblastoma. In a multicenter investigation, Liu et al [2] employed magnetic resonance imaging to build and evaluate a machine learning model based on radiomics for predicting OS in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma following the maximal safe surgical resection. A total of 582 patients in all were enrolled in retroactively. The findings suggested that a radiomics model based on a deep learning segmentation performed well in predicting OS in glioblastoma following the maximal safe surgical resection. Age, Karnofsky Performance Status score, peritumoral edema, and rad-scores of the necrotic nonenhancing core are independent predictors of OS.

An end-to-end, automated method for predicting the prognosis of glioblastoma is presented in this work. One of the main advantages is the utilization of a deep learning-based segmentation pipeline, which greatly simplifies the process and guarantees reliable tumor feature extraction, providing solid input for ensuing prognostic modeling. The method produces more reliable and accurate segmentation results for medical image analysis by optimizing spatial focus, regularization, and high-quality feature extraction.

In IDH-wild-type glioblastoma, the proposed radiomics model provides a useful tool for risk categorization. Notably, because IDH-wild-type and IDH-mutant tumors differ greatly in a number of dimensions, IDH-mutant instances were purposefully excluded during model construction. Research has confirmed that these subtypes differ fundamentally in terms of biological behavior, susceptibility profiles, metabolic traits, metabolic control, tumor invasiveness, as well as responsiveness to treatment. Furthermore, patients with IDH-mutant gliomas have noticeably better prognoses than those with IDH-wild-type tumors. The exclusion of patients with IDH-mutant gliomas from the current model is further justified by this significant prognostic disparity.

Several limitations of the study should be noted: (1) the duration of clinical trial participation differed between patients, perhaps restricting the model's predictive capacity in the early stages; (2) there could be a number of unidentified or unmeasured factors that contribute to residual confounding, and a subgroup analysis was not performed; (3) the sample size was small, which decrease the statistical power; (4) the longterm follow-up was required to confirm the predictive ability.
We ensured compliance with the TITAN 2025 guidelines [3] .
